lines.text: Everything there is, from the first instant of the Big Bang to the black holes we photograph today. This is the story of the universe, and how we came to understand it.
About thirteen point eight billion years ago, all of space, time and matter began expanding from an unimaginably hot, dense state. It has been growing and cooling ever since.
Only a couple of hundred million years later, the first stars of our own galaxy, the Milky Way, were already shining.
Our nearest large neighbour, Andromeda, lies two and a half million light-years away. It is heading toward us, and one day the two galaxies will merge.
Nearly five billion years ago, a small red dwarf was born that is now the closest star to the Sun: Proxima Centauri, a little over four light-years away.
Then, about four point six billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed, and our solar system began to take shape.
Jupiter grew into the giant of the family, heavier than all the other planets together, with a storm larger than the Earth.
Mars became a cold red desert, but its dry river valleys tell us that water once flowed across it.
Closest to the Sun, little Mercury races round in just eighty-eight days, baking by day and freezing by night.
Far out, the blue ice giant Neptune formed. It would be found in 1846 by mathematics before anyone saw it in a telescope.
Beyond it, icy Pluto. Once called the ninth planet, it showed New Horizons mountains and a great heart-shaped plain.
Saturn wrapped itself in broad rings of ice. It is so light for its size that it would float in water.
At the centre, the Sun ignited, fusing hydrogen into helium. It is about halfway through its life, and its light drives every living thing on Earth.
Uranus formed too, tipped on its side so that it rolls around the Sun.
Venus, nearly Earth's twin in size, became a furnace under thick clouds, hot enough to melt lead.
Between Mars and Jupiter, the giant's pull kept a ring of rocks from ever becoming a planet. That ring is the asteroid belt.
Its largest member is Ceres, a dwarf planet first hailed as a planet when Giuseppe Piazzi spotted it in 1801.
Far beyond, Eris circles in the cold. About as large as Pluto, its discovery in 2005 forced astronomers to decide what a planet really is.
Past Neptune stretches the Kuiper belt, a vast disc of icy leftovers from the birth of the solar system.
And about four and a half billion years ago, the third planet from the Sun formed: Earth, the only world known to hold life.
Soon after, a body the size of Mars struck the young Earth, and from the debris came the Moon, which raises our tides to this day.
Around Pluto, the moon Charon formed, so large that the two circle a point in the space between them.
At Saturn, tiny Enceladus sprays jets of water into space from an ocean hidden beneath its ice.
Jupiter's Europa hides a salty ocean too, one of the most promising places to look for life beyond Earth.
Ganymede, also Jupiter's, is the largest moon of all, bigger even than the planet Mercury.
Io, squeezed by Jupiter's gravity, is the most volcanic world we know, splashed yellow, red and white with sulphur.
Saturn's Titan has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane. In 2005, the Huygens probe landed on its frozen shore.
Neptune's Triton orbits backwards, a sign it was captured from the Kuiper belt. Voyager 2 saw ice geysers there.
And Callisto, battered with craters, has one of the oldest surfaces in the solar system.
Now the story turns to us, watching the sky. Chinese astronomers recorded Halley's comet by 240 BCE, a visitor that returns about every seventy-six years.
Around the year 150, Ptolemy wrote the Almagest, putting the Earth at the centre of all things. Astronomers would follow it for fourteen centuries.
In 1054, Chinese astronomers saw a new star so bright it shone by day. Its wreckage is the Crab Nebula.
Then Nicolaus Copernicus proposed something radical: that the Earth and the planets travel around the Sun.
His book appeared in 1543, the year he died, and began to overturn the old fixed Earth at the centre.
Galileo turned a telescope on the heavens and saw the moons of Jupiter and the phases of Venus, and paid for it with house arrest.
In 1609, Johannes Kepler showed that planets move in ellipses, not circles, laying out three laws of their motion.
A year later, Galileo's Starry Messenger told the world of mountains on the Moon and countless unseen stars.
In 1687, Newton's Principia explained why: one law of gravity governs a falling apple and the circling planets.
In 1781, William Herschel found Uranus, the first planet ever discovered with a telescope.
Urbain Le Verrier worked out from Uranus's wobbling path where an unseen planet must be, and in 1846 Neptune was found right there.
He tried the trick again, proposing a planet called Vulcan inside Mercury's orbit. It never existed, and Einstein later solved the puzzle.
In the 1920s, Edwin Hubble showed that other galaxies lie far beyond our own, and that they are rushing away from us.
Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian priest and physicist, saw in Einstein's equations a universe that could be expanding from a small, dense beginning.
In 1916, Karl Schwarzschild found the first description of a black hole, a place where gravity lets nothing escape, not even light.
It came from Einstein's general relativity, which showed gravity as the bending of space and time.
Vera Rubin measured how galaxies spin and found their outer stars moving far too fast, strong evidence for unseen dark matter.
In 1929, the evidence was in: the farther a galaxy, the faster it recedes. The universe is expanding.
Two years later, Lemaitre traced that expansion back to a beginning, the idea we now call the Big Bang.
In 1933, Fritz Zwicky first suggested that most of the matter in the universe is invisible, holding the galaxies together.
Carl Sagan would bring the universe into millions of homes with his book and television series, Cosmos.
Stephen Hawking argued that black holes give off a faint glow, and his Brief History of Time brought cosmology to a vast audience.
As a student in 1967, Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted regular radio pulses from the first known pulsars, though the Nobel Prize went to her supervisor.
In 1965, Penzias and Wilson stumbled on a faint microwave glow from every direction: the afterglow of the Big Bang itself.
At the heart of our galaxy lies Sagittarius A star, a black hole four million times the mass of the Sun, finally photographed in 2022.
In 1980, Alan Guth proposed that in its first tiny fraction of a second, the universe swelled enormously.
In July 1994, astronomers watched the fragments of comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 crash into Jupiter, leaving dark scars in its clouds.
A year later came the first planet found around a star like the Sun. Thousands more are now known.
In 1998 came a shock: the expansion of the universe is speeding up, driven by something we call dark energy.
In 2006, astronomers finally defined a planet, and Pluto became a dwarf planet.
And in 2015, LIGO felt ripples in space and time from two black holes colliding, just as Einstein had predicted a century before.
From a hot, dense beginning to ripples in space itself, the universe is still telling us its story.
